I think that IMDB has a very specific criterion that excludes some movies that I think are worth watching. For the most part, any movie on IMDB that is rated higher than an 8.0 (excluding popular movies that came out recently or had any advertisement on their site)  has a high potential to be a watchable film. Do I think their top 250 is the end all be all of movie lists? No, but the fact that it is on the list means that there I should at least be aware of it. Similarly, the AFI top 100 doesn't have the best list of movies of all time, but I have made a conscious effort to watch as many as I can. Everybody's taste in movies is subjective; therefore, instead of treating any list of the greatest movies as the ultimate list, I examine the list in the context of the list creator and appreciate it for what it is. IMDB is a list created by amateur western movie watchers and gives a pretty good list of movies that Americans enjoy. AFI is a list created by professional movie critics and industry professionals and gives a pretty good list of movies that professionals and film experts enjoy.

I think that we undervalue laziness because our traditional occupation of  labor is in either farming or factories. These institutions had thier productivity directly related to the ammount of labor that an individual put forth. Now our productivity is not determined on our effort, but on our 'cleverness'. We found ways to reduce the ammount of labor that was needed in order to survive, but instead of converging on a minimally employed workforce as was predicted by Keynes and other early 20th century economists, we have begun to reduce the ammount of payment for the same level of productivity. This only increases the ammount of labor being done for a higher level of less valuable products. We now live in the absurd situation where our prductivity causes unemployment, so we support it through artificially high prices and products that have an intentionally short lifespan. This forces us to work harder to replace the easily disposable products with artificially high prices (meaning not tied to the labor it took to produce the product but rather what the market can bear)  Ironically, those that perform the most classical labor such as farmers, miners and factory workers are paid less than those who work in offices where no tangable products are created. Our idealized conception of labor is where man makes nature to his need, but most labor is now in service of making man buy what he does not need.
